# Simple Chi Square Tests to Compare Efficacy of Rifaximin vs. Herbal Treatments for SIBO

Data originating from [(Chedid, et al., 2014)](10.7453/gahmj.2014.019).

Treatment of patients with SIBO is often relegated to the off-label use of Rifaximin, which has a poor remission rate. Patients are increasingly interested in the use of alternative medicines to treat SIBO, which encourages the examination of their efficacy in comparison to current standards of care. Chedid et al. set out to examine the real-world effectiveness of herbal treatments vs. rifaximin in the remission of SIBO, as measured by repeat lactulose breath tests (LBT). The sample for this analysis consisted of EHRs from gastroenterology patients at a tertiary care gastroenterology practice.

Three hundred and ninety-six patients in were identified that met the inclusion criteria and did not meet the exclusion criteria, of which 104 completed a follow up LBT.

```{r}
#| echo: false
Patients <- 396
kept <- 104
not_kept <- (Patients - kept)

#make a pie chart using code from https://r-graph-gallery.com/128-ring-or-donut-plot.html

data<-data.frame(Group = c("Kept", "Not Kept"), count = c(kept, not_kept))
#compute percentages
data$percentage<- 100*(data$count/sum(data$count))
#compute the cumulative percentages (top of each rectange)

data$ymax = cumsum(data$percentage)

#compute the bottom of each rectange, uses the top value from the row above. 

data$ymin = c(0, head(data$ymax, n = -1))

# Compute label position, put in the middle of each bar
data$labelPosition <- (data$ymax + data$ymin) / 2

# Compute a good label
data$label <- paste0(data$Group, "\n value: ", data$count)


library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data, aes(ymax=ymax, ymin=ymin, xmax=4, xmin=3, fill=Group)) +
  geom_rect() +
  geom_text( x=2, aes(y=labelPosition, label=label, color=Group), size=4) + # x here controls label position (inner / outer)
  scale_fill_brewer(palette=4) +
  scale_color_grey(start=.5, end = .3) +
  coord_polar(theta="y") +
  xlim(c(-1, 4)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


```

Patients were originally given two open-label treatment options based on their individual treatment preference; two 200 mg rifaximin tablets three times daily (TID), or two capsules twice daily of the commercial herbal preparations; Dysobocide and FC CIdal (Biotics Rsearch Laboratories, Rosenberg Texas) or Candibactin-AR and Candibactin BR (Metagenics, Inc, Aliso Viejo, California) for 4 consecutive weeks immediately followed by a follow-up LBT.

The primary outcome was the proportion of patients in each treatment regimen who had a negative post-treatment LBT.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(kableExtra)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
library(broom)

N <- 396
#of the 396 patients identified w/ the inclusion critieria, 104 had follow-up LBTs.
n <- 104

#patients that took a 4 week herbal treatment course
nherbal <- 37
nherbal_remission <- 17
nherbal_percent <- (round(nherbal_remission/nherbal,4)*100)

#patients that took a 4 week 1200mg course of rifaximin

nrifaximin <- 67
nrifax_remission <- 23
nrifax_percent<- (round(nrifax_remission/nrifaximin, 4)*100)

#make crosstabs table

remission_rates<- data.frame(Treatment = c("Rifaximin", "Herbal"), n = c(nrifaximin, nherbal), Remission = c(nrifax_remission, nherbal_remission), 
                             Percentage_Responders = c(nrifax_percent, nherbal_percent))

remission_rates$No_Response <- c((nrifaximin- nrifax_remission), (nherbal- nherbal_remission))

remission_rates<- remission_rates |>
  select(Treatment,Remission, No_Response, n, Percentage_Responders)

remission_rates2 <- remission_rates|>
  select(Treatment,Remission, No_Response, Percentage_Responders)

remission_rates2|>
  kable(format = "html", caption = "Remission Rates for Sibo Treatments")


```

Although the herbal treatments had a higher remission rate than Rifaximin, the unequal sample sizes make it unclear if there is a statistically significant advantage to using herbal treatments compared to Rifaximin. Using a Chi-Square Test of Homogenity:

$H_{0} :$ The proportion of Rifaximin responders is equal to that of herbal treatment responders

$H_{a} :$ Between the populations, the proportions are not equal

```{r}
#| echo: false
row_labels <- c("Rifaximin", "Herbal")
col_labels <- c("Remission", "Non-Responder")

tab <- matrix(c(nrifax_remission, nherbal_remission,
                (nrifaximin - nrifax_remission),(nherbal - nherbal_remission)),
              dimnames = list(row_labels, col_labels), nrow= 2)



# Chi-square test of homogeneity
chi_res <-chisq.test(tab, correct = F)

tidy_chi <- tidy(chi_res)
kable(tidy_chi, caption = "Chi-Square Test Results")

  
```

Based on the results of the Chi-Square test, it is clear that treatment with the herbal protocols was not statistically superior to that of treatment with Rifaximin.

So how do the odds of being a responder on herbal treatments differ from those of being on rifaximin?

**Odds Ratio**

Chedid et al. chose to adjust the odds of responding to either treatment by balancing covariates across their data set. In doing so, they obtained an odds ratio of 1.85 (C.I. of 0.77-4.41, *p* = .17). Not having access to the patient-level data to perform covariate adjustment, the expected odds ratio based on the un-adjusted data is as follows:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

p_herbal <- nherbal_percent/100
p_rifax<- nrifax_percent/100

#odds of being a responder on herbal or rifaximin treatments

odds_herbal<- p_herbal/(1-p_herbal)
odds_rifax<- p_rifax/(1-p_rifax)

#odds ratio, herbal to rifaximin

odds_ratio = odds_herbal/odds_rifax


#using Fisher's exact test on the data, since 2x2 contigency table

res<- fisher.test(tab)
herbal_vs_rifax <- 1+ res$estimate


#also do so using epitools, which looks nicer
library(epitools)

or<- oddsratio(tab, method= "fisher")

#make table the other way to get odds of being an herbal responder vs. a Rifaxin responder. 
row_labels2 <- c("Herbal", "Rifaximin")
col_labels2 <- c("Remission", "Non-Responder")

tab2 <- matrix(c(nherbal_remission,nrifax_remission
               ,(nherbal - nherbal_remission),  (nrifaximin - nrifax_remission)),
              dimnames = list(row_labels2, col_labels2), nrow= 2)

or2<-oddsratio(tab2, method ="fisher")

#make nice table
or_kable_measure <- kable(or2$measure, caption = "OR of Responding to Herbal:Rifaximin")
or_kable_measure

or_kable_p.value <- kable(or2$p.value, caption = "OR of Responding to Herbal:Rifaximin")
or_kable_p.value
```

Without adjusting for covariates, the odds of responding to the herbal treatment regimine are 1.6 times greater than those of responding to Rifaximin. Though apparently greater, the increase in odds is continues to reflect statistical non-significance.

A perhaps more intuitive understanding can be drawn from the risk ratio of responding to herbal treatments, when compared to responding to rifaximin.

```{r}
#relative risk is prob being a responder in group a/prob being a responder in group b

RR_Herbal <- p_herbal/p_rifax
RR_Herbal

#confidence interval


```

The lack of statistical significance in the difference between herbal treatment and Rifaximin does not negate the potential for clinically significant differences.
